title: Too Late to Be True: Deadlines, Lifespans and Data That Is Old by the Time It Arrives

questions.question: A lidar driver is running, its heartbeat is fine, and no scans arrive. Which watch notices?
options: The discovery lease, which notices any node that has stopped working
A lifespan on the scan topic, which expires the scans that did not come
A deadline on the scan topic: the node is alive and the data is stalled, and only a watch on the stream sees that
Nothing: a node whose heartbeat arrives is working
questions.explanation: The heartbeat says the process is running. Only a deadline on the scans themselves says that scans have stopped.

questions.question: A silence has gone on for five deadlines. How many misses does the monitor report?
options: One: it is reported once per silence and not again until a message re-arms it
Five, one for each deadline that passed
One for every check made during the silence
None, until a message arrives to end the silence
questions.explanation: A miss is an event, the start of a silence. Reporting it at every check would turn one dead lidar into a thousand lines.

questions.question: What does a monitor say before any message has arrived?
options: A miss, since no message has arrived within the deadline
Nothing: a stream that has not begun has no promise yet to break
An error, since a monitor with no stream is misconfigured
A miss after one deadline has passed from when it was created
questions.explanation: The promise is about the gap between messages. Before the first message there is no gap to measure.

questions.question: A message every 0.10 s, up to 0.03 s early or late. What does a deadline of 0.10 s do, and what does 0.17 s do?
options: 992 misses in 2000 messages at 0.10 s, and none at 0.17 s
No misses at 0.10 s, and 992 at 0.17 s
992 misses at both: jitter breaks any deadline
441 misses at 0.10 s, and 124 at 0.17 s
questions.explanation: The longest gap is the period plus the jitter at both ends, 0.16 s. A deadline equal to the period is broken about every other message by jitter alone.

questions.question: A consumer takes half as fast as messages are published, with no lifespan. How old is the data it is served, by the end of ten seconds?
options: 0.02 s, the consumer's own period
0.10 s: a queue never holds more than a few messages
5.00 s: the queue only gets longer and each message served is older than the last
10.00 s, the whole run
questions.explanation: It takes one message for every two published, so the backlog grows by half the elapsed time. After ten seconds it is acting on data five seconds old.

questions.question: What does a lifespan cost?
options: Latency: each message waits for its lifespan before delivery
Memory: expired messages are kept for inspection
Nothing: only messages nobody wanted are dropped
Messages: 490 of 500 expired at a lifespan of 0.1 s, and the count says how many
questions.explanation: The consumer is just as slow. It no longer sees a stale world; it sees less of the world, and the count says how much less.
